t: Construct Uniform Parity Array II — Parity and Ordering Analysis
o: Each nums1[i] may stay as is, or be replaced by nums1[i] - nums1[j] ≥ 1 for some j ≠ i (note: the difference must be positive, so only strictly smaller elements qualify as donors). We need all resulting values to share one parity. Crucially, the maximum element can never be replaced (nothing is smaller), so it keeps its parity. Analysis: all-even requires zero odds (the smallest odd can never become even); all-odd requires every even element to have some odd element smaller than itself, i.e., min(odds) < min(evens). Example 2 [2,3]: min odd 3 > min even 2 → false. Example 1 [1,4,7]: 1 < 4 → true. Example 3 [4,6]: no odds → true.
k: The global maximum cannot be replaced, anchoring its parity.
All-even is possible iff there are no odd elements (an odd minus anything available keeps odd parity for the smallest odd).
All-odd is possible iff there are no even elements, or min(odd) < min(even) so each even can subtract a smaller odd.

a.i: Backtracking over choices (keep vs. each valid donor) verifies feasibility directly; exponential, for small n only.
s: Try target parity even, then odd.
Recursively assign index i: keep nums1[i] if parity matches, or try every j with positive difference of matching parity.
a.t: O(2^n · n) worst case — exhaustive assignment search

a.n: Approach 2: O(n) Parity and Minimum Analysis
a.i: From the structural facts (max element immovable; smallest odd stuck odd; each even needs a smaller odd donor), feasibility reduces to comparing parities and minima.
s: Split values into odds and evens.
If either list is empty, return true.
a.t: O(n) — single pass tracking two minima

w: Always present the O(n) analysis; the backtracking version is only a correctness cross-check for tiny inputs. Pitfalls: the positivity requirement nums1[i] - nums1[j] ≥ 1 (Example 2 fails precisely because 2 - 3 is negative), and remembering the maximum element cannot be replaced. Follow-up: what if differences could be taken repeatedly (chains)?
